about: The video-game profile of harness-ai: the pieces of a game's development loop, the scale each one belongs to, the engines the profile recognises, and the lines an instruction file needs for an agent to work on a game. Read by `harness game`; explained in docs/game-profile.md, where each claim carries its source.

hour.label: one hour
hour.plain: a toy or a one-hour jam: one mechanic, no document; the loop is a person starting the game and playing it after each change
stacks: web (a canvas page, or Phaser or KAPLAY, with Vite)
hour.stacks_why: text project files and a shell that can start, test and screenshot the game, with no licence to activate

jam.label: a jam or a weekend
jam.plain: a weekend or a game jam: a build that exports from the first hour, a cut list, a capture the agent looks at, credited assets
stacks: web (Phaser or KAPLAY with Vite and Playwright)
jam.stacks_why: text project files and a shell that can start, test and screenshot the game, with no licence to activate

weeks.label: weeks to months
weeks.plain: a small game built over weeks: everything of a jam, plus game rules tested headless and the same loop run by the CI
stacks: web (Phaser or three.js with Vite and Playwright)
weeks.stacks_why: text project files and a shell that can start, test and screenshot the game, with no licence to activate

pieces.label: The engine and its exact version are pinned
pieces.gives: the agent writes the API of the version the project runs, not the one it remembers
pieces.why: the version the project runs is read from its files; one vendor test found recent models no longer mix Godot 3 and 4, so the line's value is checking the API against the right documentation, not a measured gain

pieces.label: A command starts the game for a person
pieces.gives: anyone, the agent included, can hand a playable build to the owner in one line
pieces.why: the loop ends with a person playing; this command is never judged by the runner, it opens a window or a server

pieces.label: The instruction file tells the agent the engine, the loop and what done means
pieces.gives: every session starts knowing the version, the commands of the loop and that a green run is not a working game
pieces.why: these are the facts an agent cannot discover alone; `harness game instructions` proposes the lines

pieces.label: The files the engine owns are named as not to be hand-edited
pieces.gives: the agent stops breaking scenes and references by editing serialised files as text
pieces.why: hand-edited scene, prefab and meta files break references silently; the most reported pitfall after declaring a game working without running it

pieces.label: A short design with a cut list is in the repository
pieces.gives: a new idea goes to the cut list instead of into the code
pieces.why: scope is what kills small games; the cut list is the tool that says no

pieces.label: The game exports to a build a person can open
pieces.gives: a late export failure, the most repeated jam post-mortem item, is found in the first hour
pieces.why: export templates, presets and paths break at the end when nobody tried them at the start

pieces.label: A headless run boots the game and fails on errors
pieces.gives: after each change, the agent knows the game still starts, judged by the log and not only by the exit code
pieces.why: some engines exit 0 on script errors; a run is judged by its exit code, its error lines and a line the game prints once ready

pieces.label: The loop's judge is in the repository
pieces.gives: one command, `python3 .harness/game_loop.py <piece>`, runs and judges each piece the same way for the agent, a person and the CI
pieces.why: a rule the text asks for is skipped one day in ten; a program that refuses is not

pieces.label: A command writes a screenshot the agent opens
pieces.gives: the agent sees what the player would see, and fixes a visible bug from a picture
pieces.why: agents fix visible bugs from an image and not from text; headless tests pass while the screen is wrong

pieces.label: A static check parses or compiles every script
pieces.gives: a typo is caught in seconds, before the game is started
pieces.why: cheaper than a run and cannot be fooled by the game's state

pieces.label: A person played a recent build, and it is written down with the date
pieces.gives: the owner, not the agent, decides whether it is fun, and the date says how long ago
pieces.why: no run measures feel or fun; a dated playtest log is the game's equivalent of a harvest marker. How old it may be is the owner's choice; the defaults are ours, not a source's

pieces.label: Every asset has its source and licence written
pieces.gives: the game can ship: nothing in it has an unknown licence, placeholders are marked
pieces.why: an asset without a known licence cannot be published, and jams have rules on generated or premade assets

pieces.label: The game rules are tested headless
pieces.gives: rules change without breaking: logic tested apart from rendering, with a seeded random generator and a fixed timestep
pieces.why: past the prototype the code is kept; logic separated from rendering is what makes it testable without a screen

pieces.label: The CI runs the same loop
pieces.gives: nothing merges that does not boot, whoever wrote it
pieces.why: a check that only the agent runs is skipped when the agent forgets; the CI does not forget

states.n/a: not for this engine or not needed yet

godot.name: Godot
godot.owned_rule: Never hand-edit `.tscn`, `.tres`, `.import` or `.uid` files as text without keeping their ids and uids; prefer the editor, or a script that builds the scene. Move a script together with its `.uid`.
notes: Run `godot --headless --path . --import` once on a fresh clone before anything else: the class cache lives in `.godot/`, which is not committed. The import is a prerequisite, not a check: on a syntax error it can print nothing and exit 0.

Godot exits 0 on many failures (a script that does not parse, a failing import, test scripts that fail to load): a smoke run is judged by its log and by a line the game prints once ready, and a silent run fails.
The static check is gdtoolkit (`pip install "gdtoolkit==4.*"`): `gdlint` parses every script without the engine. `--check-only` gives false alarms on scripts that use an autoload.
`--headless` renders nothing: a capture opens a window. On macOS that is the only way; on a Linux CI, wrap the capture in `xvfb-run --auto-servernum` with `--rendering-driver opengl3`.
`--write-movie shots/frame.png` writes a numbered sequence, `shots/frame00000000.png` first: that is the file the capture records.
On macOS the binary is usually `/Applications/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot`: record the full path, or a `godot` on the PATH.

Export needs the editor build, the export templates of the pinned version, the preset named in `export_presets.cfg` and an existing output folder; a relative output path is relative to `project.godot`.
owner_actions: install the export templates of the pinned version
name the export preset (Web, Linux…) in the editor once

unity.name: Unity
unity.owned_rule: Never hand-edit `.unity`, `.prefab`, `.asset` or `.meta` files, never change a GUID, and add or move an asset together with its `.meta`; change scenes through the editor, an editor script run with `-executeMethod`, or an editor bridge.
notes: Unity defines no common exit code for its tools: the test run is judged by its results file (`failed="…"`), the other runs by their log.
Never combine `-quit` with `-runTests`: the editor quits before the tests finish.
Under `-nographics` the logs are off unless `-logFile` is given: pass `-logFile -` and read the log.
A Personal licence cannot be activated from the command line: the owner activates it in Unity Hub, and the CI needs the licence file as a secret (GameCI).
`-executeMethod` calls a static method of a script under `Assets/Editor/`: the smoke, capture and build methods are code the project writes once.
owner_actions: activate the licence in Unity Hub
for CI: store the licence file and the account as secrets

unreal.name: Unreal Engine
unreal.owned_rule: `.uasset` and `.umap` files are binary: never edit them, change them in the editor or through a Python editor script or a commandlet.

candidates.run: open the .uproject in the Unreal editor of the pinned version
candidates.check: build the editor target with the project's UnrealBuildTool command

notes: These commands are candidates written from the engine's documented automation tools and were not run here: confirm each on the project before recording it.
A full Unreal loop is slow (minutes per run): at the jam scale, a smoke run per change is often all the loop can afford.
owner_actions: say whether Git LFS or Perforce holds the binary assets

web.name: Web
notes: The cheapest closed loop: a dev server, a build, and a headless browser that loads the game, fails on console errors and saves a screenshot.
Have the game set a ready mark once the first frame is drawn (a `data-ready` attribute on the canvas, or a console line), so a smoke run waits for it instead of a delay.
WebGL without a GPU needs software rendering requested explicitly in Chromium; compare screenshots only in the environment that made the reference, with a tolerance.
For itch.io, the web build is a zip with `index.html` at its root and relative paths.

love.name: LÖVE
notes: LÖVE has no headless flag: a smoke run is the game started with an argument the game reads (`--smoke`) that runs a few frames and quits, with the window module off in `conf.lua` for a logic-only run.
A Lua error shows the error screen and may not change the exit code: judge the run by its log.

pygame.name: Pygame
notes: Set `SDL_VIDEODRIVER=dummy` before pygame initialises the display: the game runs with no window, and the screen surface can still be saved to a PNG, which is a real screenshot.
`--frames` and `--capture` are arguments the game reads; a few lines in the main loop make the smoke run and the capture possible.

bevy.name: Bevy
notes: Game systems are tested on an `App` with no window: `app.update()` runs one frame, then the test reads the world.
The `bevy_ci_testing` feature reads a RON file of frame-numbered events (a fixed frame time, a screenshot, an exit): a deterministic smoke run and capture.
A capture opens a window; on a Linux CI, wrap it in `xvfb-run --auto-servernum`.

lines.text: - Engine: {engine} {version}, pinned in `{version_file}`. Check an API against the documentation of this version, not from memory; never upgrade the engine without the owner. Why: an API from another version compiles nowhere or behaves differently. (unverified) [{month}]
- After each change, the owner plays it: start the game with `{run_cmd}` and say what to try. Why: at this scale a person playing is the whole loop. (unverified) [{month}]

- After each change, run `{loop_all}`; it judges each run by its exit code, its error lines and the game's ready line. A green run is not a working game. Why: a headless run passes while the screen is wrong. {enforced} [{month}]
- Before saying a visible change is done, run `{capture_cmd}` and open `{capture_output}`. Why: a visible bug is found by looking, not by reading code. (unverified) [{month}]
- Never judge a {engine} run by its exit code alone: it exits 0 on script errors. Why: a broken scene looks like a pass. {judge_enforced} [{month}]
- {owned_rule} Why: hand-edited engine files break references without an error. (unverified) [{month}]

- Feel, difficulty and fun are the owner's call: propose values, never declare them right, and end each report with "not yet played by a person" until the owner has played. Why: no run measures them. (unverified) [{month}]
- This is a prototype: no coverage target, no refactoring, no architecture rule until the owner says the core loop is kept. Why: prototype code is meant to be thrown away. (unverified) [{month}]

- Game rules live in code that does not import the renderer, with one seeded random generator and a fixed timestep, so `{test_cmd}` runs them headless. Why: logic tied to the screen cannot be tested. (unverified) [{month}]
- A new idea goes to the cut list of `{scope_file}`, not into the code. Why: scope is what kills small games. (unverified) [{month}]
- Every asset added gets a line in `{credits_file}`: source, licence, author; a placeholder says so. Why: an asset with an unknown licence cannot ship. (unverified) [{month}]

forbidden.text: - Publishing the game (itch.io, Steam, a store, a production site) and using a publishing key or an engine licence. Why: the release is the owner's. (unverified) [{month}]

questions.ask: What does the player do, second by second, in one sentence?
questions.why: it is the one thing every check of the loop serves; only the owner decides it

questions.ask: Who plays the builds, and how often?
questions.why: it sets how old the last playtest may be before the loop calls it stale

questions.ask: If this is for a jam: which one, and what do its rules say about AI-generated code and assets, and premade assets?
questions.why: some jams forbid generated code or assets: an agent-built entry would be ineligible

questions.ask: Is there an art direction or a reference game for the look and the feel?
questions.why: the agent can match a reference; it cannot choose one for you

questions.ask: Where will it be released, if anywhere (itch.io, Steam, a web page, nowhere)?
questions.why: the export preset and the build format follow from it; publishing itself stays yours
